If the true label distribution is $p\in\Delta_K$ and the reported forecast is $q\in\Delta_K$, its expected score loss is $\bar S(p,q)=\sum_{j=1}^Kp_jS(q,j)$, where a term with $p_j=0$ contributes zero even when $S(q,j)=+\infty$.    $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in

derivations.claim: If $Z$ has finite range $z_1,\ldots,z_m\in C$ with probabilities $p_1,\ldots,p_m$, then each coordinate of $Z$ is a nonnegative simple function, so [F3] gives $\mathbb E Z=\sum_i p_i z_i$, a convex combination in $C$. The real finite-range random variable $\psi(Z)$ is integrable. Its positive and negative parts are nonnegative simple functions, so applying [F3] to each and subtracting their finite expectations gives $\mathbb E[\psi(Z)]=\sum_i p_i\psi(z_i)$. Joint convexity now proves $\psi(\mathbb E Z)\le\mathbb E[\psi(Z)]$ by induction on the number of positive weights: combine the first $m-1$ points into their normalized convex average, apply the induction hypothesis, then apply two-point convexity with weights $1-p_m$ and $p_m$.

For $n\ge1$ set $D_n=\{(m_1/n,\ldots,m_K/n):m_i\in\mathbb N_0,\sum_i m_i=n\}\subseteq\Delta_K$. This is a finite set with a canonical lexicographic order. For $p\in\Delta_K$, put $m_i=\lfloor np_i\rfloor$ for $i<K$ and $m_K=n-\sum_{i<K}m_i$. Then $m_K\ge0$, the coordinates sum to $n$, and the first $K-1$ coordinate errors are below $1/n$ while the last is below $(K-1)/n$. Thus some $q\in D_n$ has $\|p-q\|_2<\sqrt{K(K-1)}/n$. The product grid $D_n\times D_n$ therefore approximates every point of $C$ within $2K/n$. List its finitely many points canonically as $c_{n,1},\ldots,c_{n,m_n}$ and assign each point of $C$ to the first ball of radius $2K/n$ containing it. The cells are Borel by [F5]; replacing $Z$ on each cell by its center defines a measurable finite-range $Z_n\in C$ with $\|Z_n-Z\|_2<2K/n$ everywhere. The grid, order and assignment are explicit, so no choice axiom is used.

Step 1.1 gives $\mathbb E Z_n\in C$ for every $n$. Each coordinate of $Z_n$ and $Z$ is bounded by $1$, so dominated convergence [F4] gives $\mathbb E Z_n\to\mathbb E Z$ coordinatewise; because the coordinate constraints defining $C$ are closed, $\mathbb E Z\in C$.

By [F2], $\psi$ is uniformly continuous on $C$. Choose $\delta>0$ so that points within distance $\delta$ have $\psi$-values within $1$, and then choose $n$ with $2K/n<\delta$. The finite grid in step 1.2 is a $\delta$-net, so $|\psi(z)|\le1+\max_{c\in D_n\times D_n}|\psi(c)|$ for every $z\in C$. This is a common finite bound. Since $\|Z_n-Z\|_2\to0$, continuity gives $\psi(Z_n)\to\psi(Z)$ pointwise; [F4] then gives $\mathbb E\psi(Z_n)\to\mathbb E\psi(Z)$.
Applying step 1.1 to each $Z_n$ gives $\psi(\mathbb E Z_n)\le\mathbb E\psi(Z_n)$. By continuity of $\psi$ and steps 2.1 and 2.2, taking limits proves $\psi(\mathbb E Z)\le\mathbb E\psi(Z)$.

[[def-monotone-function]], in which *increasing* is the strict notion.

1. If $f'(x) \ge 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is
   nondecreasing on $I$.
2. If $f'(x) > 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is increasing on
   $I$.
3. If $f'(x) \le 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is
   nonincreasing on $I$.

The forecast is **fully reliable** if for every label $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq\Delta_K$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G\in B\}}G_j].$$
It is **classwise calibrated** if for every $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G_j\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G_j\in B\}}G_j].$$
For the **top-confidence calibration** condition, define $C=\max_jG_j$ and $\widehat Y=\min\{j:G_j=C\}$, so ties go to the smallest label. The forecast is top-confidence calibrated if for every Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=\widehat Y,\ C\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{C\in B\}}C].$$
A measurable function $r:\Delta_K\to\Delta_K$ is a **calibration function** for $G$ if for every $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq\Delta_K$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G\in B\}}r_j(G)].$$
When such a function is supplied and $d:\Delta_K\times\Delta_K\to[0,+\infty)$ is measurable, the **expected calibration error with discrepancy $d$** is $\eta_d=\mathbb E[d(r(G),G)]$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. Then $Z'_j$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable, takes values in $[0,1]$ everywhere, and equals $Z_j$ almost surely. By [F3], it has the same event integrals, so it remains a conditional-expectation version. Linearity shows that $\sum_jZ_j$ is a version of the conditional expectation of $\sum_j\mathbf1_{\{Y=y_j\}}=1$; the constant 1 is another version, so [F6] gives $\sum_jZ_j=1$ almost surely. Hence $\sum_jZ'_j=1$ almost surely.

For each label $j$ and rational $q\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]$, the event $\{Z'_j<q\}\in\mathcal G$ equals $X^{-1}(A_{j,q})$ for some $A_{j,q}\in\Sigma_X$ by [F5]. AC permits choosing these sets for the countable family of label-rational pairs. Define $\tilde\eta_j(x)=\inf(\{q\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]:x\in A_{j,q}\}\cup\{1\})$. For $0<t\le1$, $\{x:\tilde\eta_j(x)<t\}=\bigcup_{q<t}A_{j,q}$; for $t\le0$ this sublevel set is empty and for $t>1$ it is all of $\mathsf X$. Thus each $\tilde\eta_j$ is measurable and takes values in $[0,1]$ by [F4,F7].

For every $j$ and $\omega$, the rationals $q$ satisfying $X(\omega)\in A_{j,q}$ are exactly those with $Z'_j(\omega)<q$. Their infimum is $Z'_j(\omega)$ when this value is below $1$; at value $1$ the rational set is empty and the filler $1$ gives the same value. Thus $\tilde\eta_j(X)=Z'_j$ everywhere. The measurable set $D=\{x:\sum_j\tilde\eta_j(x)=1\}$ is well-defined by [F7]. Define $\eta(x)=(\tilde\eta_1(x),\ldots,\tilde\eta_K(x))$ on $D$ and $\eta(x)=(1,0,\ldots,0)$ off $D$. Then $\eta$ is measurable, takes values in $\Delta_K$ everywhere, and $\eta_j(X)=Z'_j$ almost surely because $\sum_jZ'_j=1$ almost surely.

If $p_j>0$ and $q_j=0$ for some $j$, then [F1] gives $\bar S_{\log}(p,q)=+\infty$, while $\bar S_{\log}(p,p)=-\sum_{j:p_j>0}p_j\log p_j<\infty$ because this is a finite sum of finite terms. Thus propriety is strict in this case.

Otherwise $q_j>0$ for every $j$ with $p_j>0$. The truthful risk is finite, and cancellation on the support of $p$ gives $\bar S_{\log}(p,q)-\bar S_{\log}(p,p)=\sum_{j:p_j>0}p_j\log\frac{p_j}{q_j}.$ Applying step 1.1 to $t=q_j/p_j$ yields $\sum_{j:p_j>0}p_j\log\frac{p_j}{q_j}\ge 1-\sum_{j:p_j>0}q_j\ge0.$ If the displayed difference is zero, both nonnegative gaps in this chain are zero. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let a supervised prediction problem have a measurable instance space $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$, finite label set $\mathcal Y=\{y_1,\ldots,y_K\}$ with distinct labels, the full power-set sigma-algebra on $\mathcal Y$, and $K\ge2$, and joint probability law $P$ on $\mathsf X\times\mathcal Y$; let $X$ and $Y$ be its coordinate random variables and let $\mathcal G=\{X^{-1}(A):A\in\Sigma_X\}$, the sigma-algebra generated by $X$. There is a measurable function $\eta=(\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_K):\mathsf X\to\Delta_K$, where $\Delta_K=\{p\in[0,1]^K:\sum_jp_j=1\}$, such that for every label index $j$ and $A\in\Sigma_X$,
$$P(X\in A,\ Y=y_j)=\mathbb E[\eta_j(X)\mathbf1_{\{X\in A\}}].$$

Let $K\ge2$, let $Y$ be a random variable into the finite label set $\{1,\ldots,K\}$ with its full power-set sigma-algebra on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, and let $G=(G_1,\ldots,G_K):\Omega\to\Delta_K$ be a measurable forecast, where $\Delta_K=\{p\in[0,1]^K:\sum_jp_j=1\}$. The forecast is **fully reliable** if for every label $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq\Delta_K$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G\in B\}}G_j].$$
It is **classwise calibrated** if for every $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G_j\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G_j\in B\}}G_j].$$
For the **top-confidence calibration** condition, define $C=\max_jG_j$ and $\widehat Y=\min\{j:G_j=C\}$, so ties go to the smallest label. The forecast is top-confidence calibrated if for every Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=\widehat Y,\ C\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{C\in B\}}C].$$
A measurable function $r:\Delta_K\to\Delta_K$ is a **calibration function** for $G$ if for every $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq\Delta_K$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G\in B\}}r_j(G)].$$
When such a function is supplied and $d:\Delta_K\times\Delta_K\to[0,+\infty)$ is measurable, the **expected calibration error with discrepancy $d$** is $\eta_d=\mathbb E[d(r(G),G)]$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable action space, meaning a set with
a specified sigma-algebra ([[def-measurable-space]]), and let
$L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to[0,+\infty]$ be a loss function whose section
$a\mapsto L(\theta,a)$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable for each $\theta$. A
randomized decision rule is a probability kernel $\delta$ from the data space
to the action space ([[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]]). Its
**risk** at $\theta$ is the extended nonnegative number
$$R(\theta,\delta)=\int_{\mathcal X}\left(\int_{\mathsf D}L(\theta,a)\,\delta(x,da)\right)P_\theta(dx).$$
The inner integral is a measurable function of $x$, by
[[lem-procedure-action-law-is-measurable]], so the outer nonnegative integral
is defined by [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]].
A deterministic measurable rule is included by taking its point-mass action
kernel. No measurability on $\Theta$ is required for this definition.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

kernel from a standard-Borel parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to a
standard-Borel data space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, where standard Borel means
measurably isomorphic to a Polish space
([[def-standard-borel-space]]). Let $\pi$ be a prior,
and let $L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to[0,+\infty]$ be jointly measurable for a
measurable action space $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$. Let $J$ be the joint prior-data
law of [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]], let $M$ be its data
marginal, and let $\Pi_x(d\theta)$ be a regular posterior distribution of
$\theta$ given $x$ (the disintegration is supplied by
[[thm-disintegration-of-a-joint-law-on-standard-borel-spaces]]).
Define posterior risk
$$q(x,a)=\int_\Theta L(\theta,a)\,\Pi_x(d\theta).$$
Suppose a measurable deterministic rule $d^*:\mathcal X\to\mathsf D$
attains the posterior minimum for $M$-almost every $x$; that is,
$q(x,d^*(x))\leq q(x,a)$ for every $a\in\mathsf D$ on one measurable

$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

Then
$$\int_E f\,d\mu=0.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is

$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

derivations.claim: By [F1], choose a measurable posterior probability kernel $\Pi_x$ on the finite label set; identify it with the measurable vector $G(x)=(\Pi_x(1),\ldots,\Pi_x(K))\in\Delta_K$. For each $x$, the posterior expected score of reporting $q$ is $\bar S(G(x),q)$, which is minimized at $q=G(x)$ by [F2]. The posterior risk of this rule is measurable by [F4], so the rule meets the measurable-minimizer hypothesis in [F6].

To apply the Bayes-risk interface to the original joint law, let $\pi_j=P(Y=j)$. For $\pi_j>0$, define $K_j(A)=P(X\in A,Y=j)/\pi_j$ on feature events $A$; for $\pi_j=0$, set $K_j=P_X$. Each $K_j$ is a probability measure, and the finite map $j\mapsto K_j$ is a probability kernel. The joint prior-data law built from prior $(\pi_j)$ and kernel $K_j$ agrees with the original joint law because for every $A$ and $j$ its $(A,j)$ mass is $P(X\in A,Y=j)$, including zero-prior labels. Consequently the Bayes-risk theorem [F6] states that the posterior rule $G$ minimizes the original expected score risk over all measurable randomized forecasts, hence over deterministic forecasts.

Now suppose $S$ is strictly proper and another measurable forecast $q$ has the same risk as $G$, whose risk is finite by hypothesis. Write $R_q(x)=\bar S(G(x),q(x))$ and $R_G(x)=\bar S(G(x),G(x))$. They are nonnegative measurable functions by [F3,F4], and posterior disintegration gives their integrals as the two risks, so both integrals are finite. By [F7], the measurable set $N=\{R_q=+\infty\}\cup\{R_G=+\infty\}$ is null. Set $\widetilde R_q=R_q$ and $\widetilde R_G=R_G$ off $N$, and set both to zero on $N$; these modified functions are measurable by [F10]. By [F8], the changes preserve their integrals: each original function is the sum of its restriction to $N^c$ and its restriction to the null set $N$. The functions $\widetilde R_q,\widetilde R_G$ are finite and integrable. By propriety, $D=\widetilde R_q-\widetilde R_G$ is nonnegative, and it is measurable by [F10]; [F9] gives $\mathbb E D=\mathbb E\widetilde R_q-\mathbb E\widetilde R_G=0$. Thus [F5] makes $D=0$ almost surely. Off $N$ this is equality of the finite posterior risks, so strict propriety in [F2] gives $q(X)=G(X)$ almost surely.

Let $K\ge2$, let $Y$ be a random variable into the finite label set $\{1,\ldots,K\}$ with its full power-set sigma-algebra on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, and let $G=(G_1,\ldots,G_K):\Omega\to\Delta_K$ be a measurable forecast, where $\Delta_K=\{p\in[0,1]^K:\sum_jp_j=1\}$. The forecast is **fully reliable** if for every label $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq\Delta_K$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G\in B\}}G_j].$$
It is **classwise calibrated** if for every $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G_j\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G_j\in B\}}G_j].$$
For the **top-confidence calibration** condition, define $C=\max_jG_j$ and $\widehat Y=\min\{j:G_j=C\}$, so ties go to the smallest label. The forecast is top-confidence calibrated if for every Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=\widehat Y,\ C\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{C\in B\}}C].$$
A measurable function $r:\Delta_K\to\Delta_K$ is a **calibration function** for $G$ if for every $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq\Delta_K$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G\in B\}}r_j(G)].$$
When such a function is supplied and $d:\Delta_K\times\Delta_K\to[0,+\infty)$ is measurable, the **expected calibration error with discrepancy $d$** is $\eta_d=\mathbb E[d(r(G),G)]$.

For an integer $K\ge2$, let $\Delta_K=\{p\in[0,1]^K:\sum_{j=1}^Kp_j=1\}$ and $C=\Delta_K\times\Delta_K\subset\mathbb R^{2K}$. Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $Z=(U,V):\Omega\to C$ be measurable, and let $\psi:C\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and jointly convex, meaning $\psi(\lambda z+(1-\lambda)w)\le\lambda\psi(z)+(1-\lambda)\psi(w)$ for all $z,w\in C$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$. Define $\mathbb E Z$ coordinatewise. Then $\mathbb E Z=(\mathbb E U,\mathbb E V)\in C$ and
$$\psi(\mathbb E U,\mathbb E V)\le\mathbb E[\psi(U,V)].$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.
For IID real $(X_n)_{n\ge1}$ with $\mathbb E|X_1|<\infty$, $S_n/n\to\mu=\mathbb EX_1$ almost surely.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. A von Neumann natural is the set of its
predecessors, $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), so it can be
used directly as an index set. Define

$$\mathbb{R}^n := \{\, x : x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\},$$

and write $x_k$ for $x(k)$, $k < n$. Two elements of $\mathbb{R}^n$ are equal
exactly when they agree at every $k < n$, functions being equal when they have
the same values. For $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ put

$$d_1(x,y) := \sum_{k<n} |x_k - y_k|, \qquad d_2(x,y) := \sqrt{\ \sum_{k<n} (x_k - y_k)^2\ }, \qquad d_\infty(x,y) := \max\{\, |x_k - y_k| : k < n \,\}.$$

All three are well defined: the finite sums are those of [[def-finite-sum]]; the
sum of squares is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]], [[lem-of-square-positive]])
so it has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]); and
$\{|x_k - y_k| : k < n\}$ is a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$, because
$n \ge 1$, so it has a maximum ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

**Then $d_1$, $d_2$ and $d_\infty$ are metrics on $\mathbb{R}^n$**
([[def-metric-space]]).

**Why $n \ge 1$.** For $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^0$ has exactly one element,
the empty function, and $d_1$ and $d_2$ are the empty sum $0$ and its root; but
$d_\infty$ would be the maximum of the empty set, which does not exist. The
hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is therefore not decoration, and it is carried by every
statement about $d_\infty$ in this library.

derivations.claim: Fix a partition $\mathcal P$. For every bin $B$ and each coordinate, the variables $\mathbf1_{\{G_i\in B\}}$, $\mathbf1_{\{G_i\in B\}}(V_i)_j$, and $\mathbf1_{\{G_i\in B\}}(G_i)_j$ are bounded iid real variables: the same measurable coordinate map is applied to each iid pair, so the outputs have the same law by taking preimages, and their independence follows from [F3]. Their sample averages therefore converge almost surely to their expectations. On the event $P(G\in B)>0$, division by $N_B/n\to P(G\in B)$ gives convergence of the bin means to $\mathbb E[V\mid G\in B]$ and $\mathbb E[G\mid G\in B]$. On a zero-probability bin every sample has count zero almost surely. Since the partition and label set are finite, these convergences hold together almost surely; continuity of $d$ then gives $\widehat E_{n,\mathcal P}\to E_{\mathcal P}$. By [F1], $\mathbb E[V\mid G\in B]=\mathbb E[r(G)\mid G\in B]$ coordinatewise.

Let $\delta_m$ be the maximum Euclidean diameter of a cell of $\mathcal P_m$. For any fixed $v\in\Delta_K$, the function $\psi(u,w)=\|u-w\|_2$ is continuous and jointly convex: the metric triangle inequality gives continuity in $(u,w)$, and
$$\|\lambda(u-w)+(1-\lambda)(u'-w')\|_2\le\lambda\|u-w\|_2+(1-\lambda)\|u'-w'\|_2$$
for $0\le\lambda\le1$ by the triangle inequality and homogeneity in [F5]. For a positive-probability bin $B$, define $P_B(A)=P(A\cap\{G\in B\})/P(G\in B)$. If $G(\omega)\in B$, apply [F2] under $P_B$ to the simplex pair $(G,G(\omega))$. It gives $\|\mathbb E[G\mid G\in B]-G(\omega)\|_2\le\mathbb E[\|G-G(\omega)\|_2\mid G\in B]\le\delta_m$. Apply the same argument to $(r(G),r(G(\omega)))$ to obtain $\|\mathbb E[r(G)\mid G\in B]-r(G(\omega))\|_2\le L\delta_m$. Thus the Euclidean distance between the ordered pairs is at most $\sqrt{1+L^2}\,\delta_m\le(1+L)\delta_m$. By [F4], $d$ is uniformly continuous on the compact product simplex, so the absolute difference between the bin value and $d(r(G(\omega)),G(\omega))$ is bounded by a modulus tending to zero with $\delta_m$, uniformly over all bins and $\omega$. Integrating over bins yields $E_{\mathcal P_m}\to\mathbb E[d(r(G),G)]$.

For the underestimation conclusion assume additionally that $d$ is jointly convex. For each positive-probability bin define the conditional probability measure $P_B(A)=P(A\cap\{G\in B\})/P(G\in B)$. Under $P_B$, the pair $(r(G),G)$ takes values in $\Delta_K\times\Delta_K$. Apply [F2] to $\psi=d$ and multiply by $P(G\in B)$ to obtain $P(G\in B)d\!\left(\mathbb E[r(G)\mid G\in B],\mathbb E[G\mid G\in B]\right)\le\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G\in B\}}d(r(G),G)].$ Summing over the partition proves $E_{\mathcal P}\le\mathbb E[d(r(G),G)]$.

For each fixed $m$, step 1.1 gives the almost-sure limit in $n$. There are countably many $m$, so the intersection of these probability-one events still has probability one; step 1.2 then gives the iterated limit as stated. This order takes the sample-size limit before the partition refinement and makes no claim about a jointly chosen diagonal sequence.

Let $Y$ be a random variable into $\{1,\ldots,K\}$ with its full power-set sigma-algebra, $K\ge2$, and let $G\in\Delta_K$ be a random forecast with measurable calibration function $r:\Delta_K\to\Delta_K$. Let $d:\Delta_K\times\Delta_K\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous and satisfy $d(p,p)=0$. For a finite data-independent Borel partition $\mathcal P$ of $\Delta_K$, draw an iid sequence $(G_i,Y_i)$ from the joint law of $(G,Y)$, let $V_i=e_{Y_i}$ be the corresponding standard basis vector, and form the empirical estimator
$$\widehat E_{n,\mathcal P}=\sum_{B\in\mathcal P}\frac{N_B}{n}\,d(\bar V_B,\bar G_B),$$
where $N_B=\#\{i\le n:G_i\in B\}$ and, when $N_B>0$, $\bar V_B$ and $\bar G_B$ are the sample averages in bin $B$; when $N_B=0$, set both to any fixed $q_0\in\Delta_K$. Define
$$E_{\mathcal P}=\sum_{B\in\mathcal P:P(G\in B)>0}P(G\in B)\,d\!\left(\mathbb E[r(G)\mid G\in B],\mathbb E[G\mid G\in B]\right).$$
For each fixed $\mathcal P$, $\widehat E_{n,\mathcal P}\to E_{\mathcal P}$ almost surely. If $d$ is additionally jointly convex, then $E_{\mathcal P}\le\mathbb E[d(r(G),G)]$. Without requiring convexity, if $\mathcal P_m$ is a sequence of finite data-independent Borel partitions whose mesh $\max_{B\in\mathcal P_m}\operatorname{diam}_2(B)$ tends to zero, where $\operatorname{diam}_2(B)=\sup_{u,v\in B}\|u-v\|_2$, and $r$ is Lipschitz with respect to the Euclidean metric on $\Delta_K$, then $E_{\mathcal P_m}\to\mathbb E[d(r(G),G)]$. Thus the iterated limit $\lim_{m\to\infty}\lim_{n\to\infty}\widehat E_{n,\mathcal P_m}$ equals the expected calibration error almost surely; no diagonal rate is asserted.

Assume AC. Let a supervised prediction problem have a measurable instance space $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$, finite label set $\mathcal Y=\{y_1,\ldots,y_K\}$ with distinct labels, the full power-set sigma-algebra on $\mathcal Y$, and $K\ge2$, and joint probability law $P$ on $\mathsf X\times\mathcal Y$; let $X$ and $Y$ be its coordinate random variables and let $\mathcal G=\{X^{-1}(A):A\in\Sigma_X\}$, the sigma-algebra generated by $X$. There is a measurable function $\eta=(\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_K):\mathsf X\to\Delta_K$, where $\Delta_K=\{p\in[0,1]^K:\sum_jp_j=1\}$, such that for every label index $j$ and $A\in\Sigma_X$,
$$P(X\in A,\ Y=y_j)=\mathbb E[\eta_j(X)\mathbf1_{\{X\in A\}}].$$

For a supervised prediction problem with joint law $P$, the **population risk** of any measurable predictor $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ (in particular, every $f\in\mathcal F$) is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_P(f):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(f(x),y)\,P(d(x,y))\in[0,+\infty].$$
For an ordered sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_m,y_m))$ of length $m\ge1$, the **empirical risk** or **training risk** of any such $f$ is
$$\widehat R_S(f):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\ell(f(x_i),y_i)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Neither definition assumes finite risk. The sum uses extended nonnegative arithmetic; since $m\ge1$, any summand equal to $+\infty$ makes the empirical risk $+\infty$.

Let $Y\in\{-1,+1\}$ be the label in a supervised prediction problem with the full power-set sigma-algebra on this binary label set, and choose the finite-label conditional probability function ordered as $(-1,+1)$; write $\eta(x)=\eta_{+1}(x)$. Let $\Phi:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$ be finite, convex and nondecreasing. It is continuous on $\mathbb R$; extend it to $\overline{\mathbb R}=\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\}$ by its one-sided monotone limits, which may equal $+\infty$. The resulting extended function is Borel measurable. For $u\in\overline{\mathbb R}$ define the conditional margin risk
$$L_\Phi(x,u)=\eta(x)\Phi(-u)+(1-\eta(x))\Phi(u),$$
using $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ at endpoints. A measurable extended-real conditional minimizer is a measurable $h_\Phi^*:\mathsf X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ satisfying $L_\Phi(x,h_\Phi^*(x))\le L_\Phi(x,u)$ for every $x$ and every $u\in\overline{\mathbb R}$. For a measurable real-valued score $h$, its margin loss is $\ell_\Phi(h(x),y)=\Phi(-yh(x))$, its surrogate risk is $L_\Phi(h)=\mathbb E[\Phi(-Yh(X))]$, and its conditional-minimum risk is $L_\Phi^*=\mathbb E[L_\Phi(X,h_\Phi^*(X))]$. Under the zero-score-is-error convention, its classification risk is $R_{01}(h)=P(Yh(X)\le0)$, and the Bayes classification risk is $R_{01}^*=\mathbb E[\min\{\eta(X),1-\eta(X)\}]$. Write $h^*(x)=\eta(x)-\tfrac12$ for the centered conditional class probability.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

derivations.claim: Put $A_- = \{x:h(x)\le0\}$ and $A_+ = \{x:h(x)\ge0\}$, which are measurable by [F3]. The event $\{Yh(X)\le0\}$ is the disjoint union of $\{Y=+1,X\in A_-\}$ and $\{Y=-1,X\in A_+\}$. Applying [F1] to $A_-$ and using $P(X\in A_+,Y=-1)=P(X\in A_+)-P(X\in A_+,Y=+1)$ gives $R_{01}(h)=\mathbb E[\eta(X)\mathbf1_{A_-}(X)+(1-\eta(X))\mathbf1_{A_+}(X)].$ Subtracting [F2]'s Bayes-risk integrand reduces the identity to a pointwise comparison for each $x$.

Fix $x$ and abbreviate $a=\eta(x)$. If $a>1/2$, then on $h(x)>0$ the conditional risk is $1-a$ and the excess is zero; on $h(x)<0$ it is $a$, so the excess is $2a-1=2|a-1/2|$; on $h(x)=0$ it is $1$, so the excess is $a=(2a-1)+(1-a)$. If $a<1/2$, the same three cases $h(x)<0$, $h(x)>0$, and $h(x)=0$ give excesses $0$, $1-2a=2|a-1/2|$, and $1-a=(1-2a)+a$, respectively. If $a=1/2$, every nonzero score has excess zero and a zero score has excess $1/2$. In each case the excess equals $2|a-1/2|\mathbf1_{\{h(x)(a-1/2)\le0\}}+\min(a,1-a)\mathbf1_{\{h(x)=0\}}$.
Integrating the pointwise equality in step 2.1 and using step 1.1 proves the displayed risk identity.

The right side of the identity is nonnegative, so every measurable score has risk at least $R_{01}^*$. Define $h_B(x)=+1$ when $\eta(x)\ge1/2$ and $h_B(x)=-1$ otherwise. Its two level sets are measurable by [F3]; at each $x$, its conditional zero-one risk is $\min\{\eta(x),1-\eta(x)\}$, including equality at $\eta=1/2$. Thus $R_{01}(h_B)=R_{01}^*$, verifying that the stated Bayes risk is the attained infimum.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The forecast is **fully reliable** if for every label $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq\Delta_K$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G\in B\}}G_j].$$
It is **classwise calibrated** if for every $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G_j\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G_j\in B\}}G_j].$$
For the **top-confidence calibration** condition, define $C=\max_jG_j$ and $\widehat Y=\min\{j:G_j=C\}$, so ties go to the smallest label. The forecast is top-confidence calibrated if for every Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=\widehat Y,\ C\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{C\in B\}}C].$$
A measurable function $r:\Delta_K\to\Delta_K$ is a **calibration function** for $G$ if for every $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq\Delta_K$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G\in B\}}r_j(G)].$$
When such a function is supplied and $d:\Delta_K\times\Delta_K\to[0,+\infty)$ is measurable, the **expected calibration error with discrepancy $d$** is $\eta_d=\mathbb E[d(r(G),G)]$.

In each model the three forecast vectors are distinct. Therefore full reliability would require $p_i=g_i$ at every row by [F1], but Model A row 1, Model B row 1, and Model C row 1 each have $p_i\ne g_i$. Full reliability fails in all three models.

In Model A, for each label the groups with forecast coordinate $0.4$ have conditional frequency $0.4$, and the groups with coordinate $0.3$ have average conditional frequency $0.3$: for labels 1, 2, and 3 the latter averages are respectively $(0.2+0.4)/2$, $(0.4+0.2)/2$, and $(0.2+0.4)/2$. Thus Model A is classwise calibrated. Its top confidence is always $0.4$, its predicted labels are $1,2,3$ in the three rows, and each corresponding conditional correctness probability is $0.4$, so it is top-confidence calibrated.

In Model B the top confidence is always $0.5$, the predicted labels are $1,2,3$, and the average conditional correctness is $(0.7+0.5+0.3)/3=0.5$, so top-confidence calibration holds. Classwise calibration fails because forecast coordinate $G_1=0.5$ occurs only in row 1, where $P(Y=1\mid X=1)=0.7\ne0.5$.

In Model C, for each label the forecast coordinate $0.5$ group has average conditional frequency $0.5$, and the coordinate $0$ group has frequency $0$: the three nonzero-group averages are $(0.8+0.2)/2$, $(0.2+0.8)/2$, and $(0.8+0.2)/2$. $$\widehat E_{n,\mathcal P}=\sum_{B\in\mathcal P}\frac{N_B}{n}\,d(\bar V_B,\bar G_B),$$
